Vgs8-_XG2aw.title: Tafseer of Surat 'Abasa, Part 2: Verses 17-32
Vgs8-_XG2aw.one_line: Reviewing the frown story in 'Abasa as Islam's ethical bar, then reading 80:17-32 as the Quran's lesson on gratitude as a debt owed.
Vgs8-_XG2aw.summary: He places 'Abasa within the opening of Juz Amma: An-Naba' gives Allah's account of existence, An-Nazi'at the tools of the self, and 'Abasa the ethical standard, since Islam is at its core a moral code. He retells the story of the Prophet turning from a powerful, condescending Qurayshi leader to the blind companion Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, with only a momentary frown that no one saw. Allah still revealed it, which shows how high the bar is: you may not frown, even for a noble reason, at someone who cannot see it. He argues the surah is evidence of prophethood, because no deceiver adds to the work needed to win trust. The bar does not drop under stress, and the Quran, carried in honoured pages by noble angels, is a gift to be valued or returned. The second section gives gratitude as the model value. Kufr at root is denying a blessing and refusing to credit its giver. Created from a drop, guided, then returned and raised, the human being has not yet paid his debt of gratitude. Look at your food: water poured, earth split, a rich variety grown for you and your animals. He asks people to count their countless blessings while still working on their problems.

outline.heading: Measurable societal change from the last juz
outline.gist: Sociology struggles to measure change, but the transformation the Prophet brought is visible in poetry, governance and education, rooted in the last juz.

outline.heading: Juz Amma's first surahs: Allah's account of existence and the tools of the self
outline.gist: An-Naba' gives the perspective of the one who set the way of life; An-Nazi'at describes the self as both the tool and the obstacle.

outline.heading: Is morality part of an ideology? Islam as a moral code
outline.gist: Some ideologies treat morality as optional; Islam's defining feature is its ethical standard, which 'Abasa sets out.

outline.heading: A surah named by a verb: He frowned
outline.gist: The surah has three parts, and its name is a complete verb, which invites the question of what a frown has to do with revelation.

outline.heading: The hardest kind of da'wah: a powerful, contemptuous listener
outline.gist: Early on the Prophet argued with leaders who looked down on him while Quraysh prospered on corruption and saw no need for change.

outline.heading: Injustice in your favour: the classroom points experiment
outline.gist: Youth given unfair points only objected when the unfairness hurt them; Quraysh were likewise the beneficiaries of the injustice around them.

outline.heading: Quraysh saw where the message led
outline.gist: The leaders knew it would topple their position, so the Prophet was arguing uphill against everything; he admits he gave up on that kind of da'wah himself.

outline.heading: Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum calls out
outline.gist: The blind companion, eager for knowledge, approaches; the Prophet wants to stay with the harder, nobler task of winning a leader who could protect the tortured Muslims.

outline.heading: A momentary frown no one saw, made into revelation
outline.gist: He left the leader and served the blind man fully, yet Allah revealed what had passed in his face, an incident no one would otherwise have known.

outline.heading: 'Itab: a loving reproach
outline.gist: Allah's gentle reproach, which the Prophet honoured by kissing Ibn Umm Maktum's head; spouses can point out hurt this way without a fight.

outline.heading: The ethical standard: no frown, even for a noble reason
outline.gist: Neither a good motive nor the man's blindness excuses it; perhaps the blind man would be purified and do more good than the leader.

outline.heading: The indifferent one versus the one who comes in awe
outline.gist: You are not accountable for someone who refuses purification, but you may not be distracted from the one who comes seeking with reverence.

outline.heading: Evidence of prophethood: no con man adds to his own burden
outline.gist: A deceiver never volunteers a fault that requires years of flawless character to overcome; this surah does exactly that.

outline.heading: A standard that seems out of reach, and simply a reminder
outline.gist: The surah makes the bar harder for followers, and tells him not to force guidance; it is a reminder for whoever wills.

outline.heading: Hurtful even if unseen and unintended
outline.gist: A smirk the other person never notices is still wrong; the Prophet made amends with Ibn Umm Maktum despite everything he faced.

outline.heading: The bar does not lower under stress
outline.gist: Pressure is no licence to mistreat people; Allah noticed a momentary frown, which should scare us about the small slips we never notice.

outline.heading: Honoured pages carried by noble scribes
outline.gist: The Quran is elevated and carried only by noble, virtuous angels; a Muslim should treat it as a gift, or give it back.

outline.heading: Second section: gratitude as the model value
outline.gist: After defining the standard, the surah gives gratitude as one of the most important values a Muslim carries.

outline.heading: Interlude
Perish man, how ungrateful: kufr as denying a blessing
outline.gist: Kufr at root is failing to see a blessing and refusing to credit its giver, like a teenager who takes his parents' gifts for granted.

outline.heading: Gratitude as feeling indebted
outline.gist: Gratitude is feeling blessed and owing something back; a Muslim knows exactly whom he owes.

outline.heading: From a drop, guided on the path, then death and resurrection
outline.gist: Allah created man from a drop of fluid, proportioned him, eased his path, then causes him to die and will raise him.

outline.heading: Lamma: not yet fulfilled
outline.gist: The particle lamma means something expected has not happened yet, like waiting at the meeting place for a friend still to come.

outline.heading: Humble beginnings and the unpaid debt of gratitude
outline.gist: Yaqdi means paying a debt; man, created from almost nothing and given a path, still owes his Lord gratitude.

outline.heading: Pop psychology rediscovering gratitude
outline.gist: Muslims listen when a therapist on a podcast praises gratitude but ignore the Quran that opens with alhamdulillah.

outline.heading: Interlude
Let man look at his food: water truly poured
outline.gist: Insan here means raw human nature; the doubled verb stresses the massive amounts of water poured from the sky.

outline.heading: The earth split open: grain, vines, olives, palms, gardens
outline.gist: He lists the produce growing from the split earth, gardens so dense they look dark.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr did not know what abb meant
outline.gist: The second greatest of the ummah admitted he did not know a word; knowledge should grow with each generation.

outline.heading: Same verse, different purpose: from self-value to gratitude
outline.gist: The verse on provision for you and your livestock appeared in An-Nazi'at to restore self-value; here it calls for gratitude.

outline.heading: Infinite reasons for gratitude amid real problems
outline.gist: A few things going wrong in marriage, health or money do not cancel countless blessings; be grateful while still fixing your problems.

12:47.ar: قَالَ تَزۡرَعُونَ سَبۡعَ سِنِينَ دَأَبࣰ ا فَمَا حَصَدتُّمۡ فَذَرُوهُ فِي سُنۢبُلِهِۦٓ إِلَّا قَلِيلࣰ ا مِّمَّا تَأۡكُلُونَ
12:47.en: He said: Ye shall sow seven years as usual, but that which ye reap, leave it in the ear, all save a little which ye eat

12:48.ar: ثُمَّ يَأۡتِي مِنۢ بَعۡدِ ذَٰلِكَ سَبۡعࣱ شِدَادࣱ يَأۡكُلۡنَ مَا قَدَّمۡتُمۡ لَهُنَّ إِلَّا قَلِيلࣰ ا مِّمَّا تُحۡصِنُونَ
12:48.en: Then after that will come seven hard years which will devour all that ye have prepared for them, save a little of that which ye have stored

12:49.ar: ثُمَّ يَأۡتِي مِنۢ بَعۡدِ ذَٰلِكَ عَامࣱ فِيهِ يُغَاثُ ٱلنَّاسُ وَفِيهِ يَعۡصِرُونَ
12:49.en: Then, after that, will come a year when the people will have plenteous crops and when they will press (wine and oil)

12:50.ar: وَقَالَ ٱلۡمَلِكُ ٱئۡتُونِي بِهِۦۖ فَلَمَّا جَآءَهُ ٱلرَّسُولُ قَالَ ٱرۡجِعۡ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ فَسۡـَٔلۡهُ مَا بَالُ ٱلنِّسۡوَةِ ٱلَّٰتِي قَطَّعۡنَ أَيۡدِيَهُنَّۚ إِنَّ رَبِّي بِكَيۡدِهِنَّ عَلِيمࣱ‏
12:50.en: And the king said: Bring him unto me. And when the messenger came unto him, he (Joseph) said: Return unto thy lord and ask him what was the case of the women who cut their hands. Lo! my Lord knoweth their guile

12:51.ar: قَالَ مَا خَطۡبُكُنَّ إِذۡ رَٰوَدتُّنَّ يُوسُفَ عَن نَّفۡسِهِۦۚ قُلۡنَ حَٰشَ لِلَّهِ مَا عَلِمۡنَا عَلَيۡهِ مِن سُوٓءࣲۚ قَالَتِ ٱمۡرَأَتُ ٱلۡعَزِيزِ ٱلۡـَٰٔنَ حَصۡحَصَ ٱلۡحَقُّ أَنَا۠ رَٰوَدتُّهُۥ عَن نَّفۡسِهِۦ وَإِنَّهُۥ لَمِنَ ٱلصَّٰدِقِينَ
12:51.en: He (the king) (then sent for those women and) said: What happened when ye asked an evil act of Joseph? They answered: Allah Blameless! We know no evil of him. Said the wife of the ruler: Now the truth is out. I asked of him an evil act, and he is surely of the truthful

12:52.ar: ذَٰلِكَ لِيَعۡلَمَ أَنِّي لَمۡ أَخُنۡهُ بِٱلۡغَيۡبِ وَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَهۡدِي كَيۡدَ ٱلۡخَآئِنِينَ
12:52.en: (Then Joseph said: I asked for) this, that he (my lord) may know that I betrayed him not in secret, and that surely Allah guideth not the snare of the betrayers

12:53.ar: ۞وَمَآ أُبَرِّئُ نَفۡسِيٓۚ إِنَّ ٱلنَّفۡسَ لَأَمَّارَةُۢ بِٱلسُّوٓءِ إِلَّا مَا رَحِمَ رَبِّيٓۚ إِنَّ رَبِّي غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
12:53.en: I do not exculpate myself. Lo! the (human) soul enjoineth unto evil, save that whereon my Lord hath mercy. Lo! my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful

6:70.en: And forsake those who take their religion for a pastime and a jest, and whom the life of the world beguileth. Remind (mankind) hereby lest a soul be destroyed by what it earneth. It hath beside Allah no protecting ally nor intercessor, and though it offer every compensation it will not be accepted from it. Those are they who perish by their own deserts. For them is drink of boiling water and a painful doom, because they disbelieved

57:12.ar: يَوۡمَ تَرَى ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ وَٱلۡمُؤۡمِنَٰتِ يَسۡعَىٰ نُورُهُم بَيۡنَ أَيۡدِيهِمۡ وَبِأَيۡمَٰنِهِمۖ بُشۡرَىٰكُمُ ٱلۡيَوۡمَ جَنَّٰتࣱ تَجۡرِي مِن تَحۡتِهَا ٱلۡأَنۡهَٰرُ خَٰلِدِينَ فِيهَاۚ ذَٰلِكَ هُوَ ٱلۡفَوۡزُ ٱلۡعَظِيمُ
57:12.en: On the day when thou (Muhammad) wilt see the believers, men and women, their light shining forth before them and on their right hands, (and wilt hear it said unto them): Glad news for you this day: Gardens underneath which rivers flow, wherein ye are immortal. That is the supreme triumph

57:13.ar: يَوۡمَ يَقُولُ ٱلۡمُنَٰفِقُونَ وَٱلۡمُنَٰفِقَٰتُ لِلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ ٱنظُرُونَا نَقۡتَبِسۡ مِن نُّورِكُمۡ قِيلَ ٱرۡجِعُواْ وَرَآءَكُمۡ فَٱلۡتَمِسُواْ نُورࣰ اۖ فَضُرِبَ بَيۡنَهُم بِسُورࣲ لَّهُۥ بَابُۢ بَاطِنُهُۥ فِيهِ ٱلرَّحۡمَةُ وَظَٰهِرُهُۥ مِن قِبَلِهِ ٱلۡعَذَابُ
57:13.en: On the day when the hypocritical men and the hypocritical women will say unto those who believe: Look on us that we may borrow from your light! it will be said: Go back and seek for light! z-lEvTDm2To.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Yusuf 12:47-53
z-lEvTDm2To.one_line: Yusuf refuses to trade sacred knowledge for his release, demands his name be cleared, and the wife of al-Aziz confesses.
z-lEvTDm2To.summary: He opens by stressing that Egypt was the heart of the ancient world, so its famine would have ruined humanity, and argues that the prophets named in the Quran are those around whom human history turned. Guidance, he says, is a basic human need distinct from science, wealth or technology: science cannot say why we have what we have, and his years in oncology confirmed what scholars taught, that people without meaning collapse once their distractions stop. Humanity invented intoxicants, gambling and endless entertainment to avoid that question. Yusuf's plan of seven good years followed by seven hard ones mirrors life: plant now for the hard Day ahead. The core lesson is that Yusuf, forgotten in prison for years, gave the interpretation at once without bargaining, because divine knowledge is not sold or used as leverage. He links this to his objection to paid Quran classes and to aggressive fundraising, citing the prophets who asked no wage and his own teacher who refused payment. Only when summoned for himself did Yusuf negotiate, insisting the women be questioned so he would leave with his name cleared. The wife of al-Aziz then confesses; she never betrayed the truth within herself and did not absolve her soul.

outline.heading: Egypt as the centre of the ancient world
outline.gist: Its collapse in famine would have meant the ruin of the surrounding world.

outline.heading: Why the Quran names these twenty-five prophets
outline.gist: They are the prophets around whom human history turned.

outline.heading: Prophets who changed the course of history
outline.gist: Without them civilisation would not be what it is; every prophet who shaped history is in the Quran.

outline.heading: Guidance is not science, wealth or power
outline.gist: Prophets came when people most needed guidance, which differs from progress.

outline.heading: Having something versus knowing what to do with it
outline.gist: Without guidance a person stays restless and thirsty whatever he owns.

outline.heading: Science cannot answer why
outline.gist: Empirical science does not ask why we have our abilities or where we are heading.

outline.heading: Every need met, and then aging and death
outline.gist: A thought experiment: with all needs met one still faces aging, death and the question of meaning.

outline.heading: Guidance as a basic human need
outline.gist: Remove it and people lose the capacity to continue and to find purpose.

outline.heading: What his oncology work taught him
outline.gist: Life ends in death without escape, exactly as the scholars said.

outline.heading: Time respects no one
outline.gist: Years taken from Yusuf in prison were never returned; we notice death as peers begin to die.

outline.heading: The busy man who collapses when idle
outline.gist: A wealthy, travelling patient breaks down when he finally sits and thinks.

outline.heading: We invented distractions
outline.gist: Humans, not Shaytan, created endless screens and noise to avoid thinking about our lives.

outline.heading: Intoxicants and gambling in every nation
outline.gist: Every civilisation invented wine and gambling early to switch off the questioning mind.

outline.heading: Prophets explain purpose; religion turned into folklore
outline.gist: People prefer religion as play and festive culture without obligations.

outline.heading: Yusuf, Musa and Ibrahim as turning points
outline.gist: Each brought guidance and also rescued people from collapse.

outline.heading: Yusuf gives the full plan at once
outline.gist: Plant, leave the grain in the ear, store it, and ration through the hard years.

outline.heading: Seven easy years and seven hard ones: a picture of life
outline.gist: Now prayers and repentance are accepted; prepare now for the hard Day.

outline.heading: Seven as a sign of continuity
outline.gist: Arabs used seven for permanence, as in the week and the seven circuits of tawaf.

outline.heading: On the Day you eat what you sent ahead
outline.gist: Light on the bridge depends on what was planted in this life.

outline.heading: The king hears the interpretation
outline.gist: He realises the interpreter is no ordinary man and summons him.

outline.heading: Forgotten for years, he did not take the chance
outline.gist: No lawyer or family outside, yet he did not use the dream to win his freedom.

outline.heading: Personal grievance versus divine knowledge
outline.gist: Yusuf keeps his right to defend himself separate from knowledge Allah gave him.

outline.heading: Knowledge is given to friend and foe alike
outline.gist: In prison he called to Allah first without being asked; sacred knowledge is not traded.

outline.heading: No price on the Quran
outline.gist: He founded the centre partly to show that Quran teaching should not be sold.

outline.heading: Every prophet asked no wage
outline.gist: The Quran repeats that prophets asked no payment, lest people be burdened.

outline.heading: Payment teaches that the Quran has a price
outline.gist: Charging makes people imagine divine knowledge can be bought.

outline.heading: His sheikh refuses his father's gift
outline.gist: After he completed his first khatmah, his teacher was offended at being offered money.

outline.heading: Not even a registration fee
outline.gist: Donate to the masjid generally, but never tie a fee to Quran or Sunnah lessons.

outline.heading: Fundraising that pressures the audience
outline.gist: Nearly every gathering now includes long pleas for money, which he finds exhausting.

outline.heading: Praise for Yaqeen, criticism of the pitch
outline.gist: He values Yaqeen and Sh. Omar Suleiman but objects to the pressured pledge style; the Prophet simply laid out his cloak.

outline.heading: A borrowed model; find an alternative
outline.gist: The fundraising-dinner model is a Western invention; he does not know the alternative but says one must be found.

outline.heading: Money erodes respect for scholars
outline.gist: A student who pays treats his teacher as an employee; early scholars condemned reciters who sought the doors of the powerful.

ALUXh-l7NpI.title: Deeds Rendered Unacceptable #2: Raising Your Voice
ALUXh-l7NpI.one_line: Surat al-Hujurat's warning against raising voices over the Prophet, the story of Thabit ibn Qays, and respect for teachers and scholars.
ALUXh-l7NpI.summary: Asked twice about it, he places the verse of al-Hujurat within his series on deeds that lose their reward: believers must not raise their voices above the Prophet's or call him by name as they call one another, lest their deeds become void without their noticing. He notes that people often think a louder voice makes a better argument. He tells the story of Thabit ibn Qays, a man with a naturally loud voice, who stayed home weeping, convinced his deeds were lost and he was bound for the Fire; when the Prophet learned of it he sent word that Thabit was among the people of Paradise. He argues Thabit's remorse is itself why he was saved. Scholars draw from this that a lack of etiquette can forfeit reward, with the Prophet first, and by extension with parents, teachers, scholars and elders: do not raise your voice in their presence or call them by first name. He gives his own example of a hospital mentor he cannot bring himself to call by first name, and says he notices disrespect toward elders and scholars in the community. That chain of respect, passed from the companions to the scholars, is what lets a community innovate positively while keeping authentic scholarship.

full.full_ar: يروي الإمام البخاري في صحيحه (4846) قال: حَدَّثَنَا عَلِيُّ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ، حَدَّثَنَا أَزْهَرُ بْنُ سَعْدٍ، أَخْبَرَنَا ابْنُ عَوْنٍ، قَالَ أَنْبَأَنِي مُوسَى بْنُ أَنَسٍ، عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ رضي الله عنه: «أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صلى الله عليه وسلم افْتَقَدَ ثَابِتَ بْنَ قَيْسٍ فَقَالَ رَجُلٌ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ أَنَا أَعْلَمُ لَكَ عِلْمَهُ. فَأَتَاهُ فَوَجَدَهُ جَالِسًا فِي بَيْتِهِ مُنَكِّسًا رَأْسَهُ فَقَالَ لَهُ مَا شَأْنُكَ. فَقَالَ شَرٌّ. كَانَ يَرْفَعُ صَوْتَهُ فَوْقَ صَوْتِ النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَقَدْ حَبِطَ عَمَلُهُ، وَهْوَ مِنْ أَهْلِ النَّارِ. فَأَتَى الرَّجُلُ النَّبِيَّ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَأَخْبَرَهُ أَنَّهُ قَالَ كَذَا وَكَذَا ـ فَقَالَ مُوسَى ـ فَرَجَعَ إِلَيْهِ الْمَرَّةَ الآخِرَةَ بِبِشَارَةٍ عَظِيمَةٍ فَقَالَ “اذْهَبْ إِلَيْهِ فَقُلْ لَهُ إِنَّكَ لَسْتَ مِنْ أَهْلِ النَّارِ، وَلَكِنَّكَ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْجَنَّةِ”»
full.full_en: Imam al-Bukhari narrates in his Sahih (4846): Ali ibn Abdillah (al-Madini) narrated to us from Azhar ibn Sa'd, from Ibn Awn, from Musa ibn Anas, from Anas ibn Malik: "The Prophet (peace be upon him) noticed Thabit ibn Qays was missing. A man said: O Messenger of Allah, I will find out about him for you. He went to him and found him sitting in his house with his head bowed, and asked: What is the matter with you? He said: Something bad. He used to raise his voice above the voice of the Prophet (peace be upon him), so his deeds have been nullified and he is among the people of the Fire. The man went back to the Prophet (peace be upon him) and told him he had said such and such. (Musa said:) Then the man returned to him the second time with great good news. He said: 'Go to him and say to him: You are not among the people of the Fire, but you are among the people of Paradise.'"

Qt60gmb8BX0.one_line: At-Takwir teaches that free will is a sacred, divine gift: the buried girl, Jibril and the Prophet frame what makes human choice unique.
Qt60gmb8BX0.summary: He gives his audience a compass for their own reflection: At-Takwir opens a cluster of five surahs on free will, the uniquely human margin of choice, and this surah teaches that it is a sacred, divine gift that no one may take away. Amid the cosmic upheavals of the Day, the buried baby girl is asked for what sin she was killed. She had no will, so the question is aimed at those who did. In a long aside he condemns 'big thinkers' and powers who sacrifice children and the common person, calling them casualties, and insists all man-made harm has someone responsible. Every soul then knows what it has brought: only its choices. The oaths by shooting stars, the departing night and the breathing dawn signal that the opportunity is still open and that the Quran is that morning breath. Jibril is described with every noble quality yet lacks the one thing humans have: choice. The Prophet is not mad, does not withhold revelation and is not inspired by a devil, closing every involuntary explanation for his message. Finally, the Quran is a reminder for whoever wills to go straight, yet we will only because Allah willed us to will. Like Adam, we must own our choices; he urges the young never to surrender their will.

thfqFaRysbE.title: Essentials and Pet Peeves: Acceptance of Deeds
thfqFaRysbE.one_line: The fear of deeds being voided (habt): the outward and inward conditions of acceptance and why a Muslim keeps striving until death.
thfqFaRysbE.summary: He explains that the series covers essentials, basic givens of Islam that many young Muslims were never taught. Opening with the verses on the greatest losers in deeds, he describes the biggest loser as someone who expected the highest ranks of paradise and finds himself in the worst of hell, because he believed he was doing well. The key word is habt: a deed that looks correct but carries no reward. He shows the theme across the Quran and Sunnah: the warning in Al-Hujurat that raising voices above the Prophet's voids deeds without one noticing, Thabit ibn Qays fearing he was among the people of hell, the man who swore Allah would not forgive another, the verses in Surat Muhammad about disbelievers' deeds being voided, and the hadith of people arriving with deeds like the mountains of Tihamah that Allah turns to scattered dust because they violated His limits in private. In the second khutbah he divides the conditions of acceptance into outward ones, learning the fiqh of every act, for which no one has an excuse, and inward ones such as adab and intention. Since no one can swear a deed was accepted, the believer keeps a measure of fear, renews his intention, perfects his work and hopes that one deed in his life is accepted.

89:16.en: But whenever He trieth him by straitening his means of life, he saith: My Lord despiseth me

16:97.ar: مَنۡ عَمِلَ صَٰلِحࣰ ا مِّن ذَكَرٍ أَوۡ أُنثَىٰ وَهُوَ مُؤۡمِنࣱ فَلَنُحۡيِيَنَّهُۥ حَيَوٰةࣰ طَيِّبَةࣰۖ وَلَنَجۡزِيَنَّهُمۡ أَجۡرَهُم بِأَحۡسَنِ مَا كَانُواْ يَعۡمَلُونَ
16:97.en: Whosoever doeth right, whether male or female, and is a believer, him verily we shall quicken with good life, and We shall pay them a recompense in proportion to the best of what they used to do

29:64.ar: وَمَا هَٰذِهِ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنۡيَآ إِلَّا لَهۡوࣱ وَلَعِبࣱۚ وَإِنَّ ٱلدَّارَ ٱلۡأٓخِرَةَ لَهِيَ ٱلۡحَيَوَانُۚ لَوۡ كَانُواْ يَعۡلَمُونَ
29:64.en: This life of the world is but a pastime and a game. Lo! the home of the Hereafter - that is Life, if they but knew

38:44.ar: وَخُذۡ بِيَدِكَ ضِغۡثࣰ ا فَٱضۡرِب بِّهِۦ وَلَا تَحۡنَثۡۗ إِنَّا وَجَدۡنَٰهُ صَابِرࣰ اۚ نِّعۡمَ ٱلۡعَبۡدُ إِنَّهُۥٓ أَوَّابࣱ‏

54:17.ar: وَلَقَدۡ يَسَّرۡنَا ٱلۡقُرۡءَانَ لِلذِّكۡرِ فَهَلۡ مِن مُّدَّكِرࣲ‏

4:69.en: Whoso obeyeth Allah and the messenger, they are with those unto whom Allah hath shown favour, of the prophets and the saints and the martyrs and the righteous. The best of company are they

5:75.ar: مَّا ٱلۡمَسِيحُ ٱبۡنُ مَرۡيَمَ إِلَّا رَسُولࣱ قَدۡ خَلَتۡ مِن قَبۡلِهِ ٱلرُّسُلُ وَأُمُّهُۥ صِدِّيقَةࣱۖ كَانَا يَأۡكُلَانِ ٱلطَّعَامَۗ ٱنظُرۡ كَيۡفَ نُبَيِّنُ لَهُمُ ٱلۡأٓيَٰتِ ثُمَّ ٱنظُرۡ أَنَّىٰ يُؤۡفَكُونَ
5:75.en: The Messiah, son of Mary, was no other than a messenger, messengers (the like of whom) had passed away before him. And his mother was a saintly woman. And they both used to eat (earthly) food. See how We make the revelations clear for them, and see how they are turned away

17:65.ar: إِنَّ عِبَادِي لَيۡسَ لَكَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ سُلۡطَٰنࣱۚ وَكَفَىٰ بِرَبِّكَ وَكِيلࣰ ا
17:65.en: Lo! My (faithful) bondmen - over them thou hast no power, and thy Lord sufficeth as (their) guardian

79KCwok324M.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Yusuf 12:42-49
79KCwok324M.one_line: Yusuf's forgotten years in prison and the king's dream: relief is not guaranteed in this life, and Yusuf answers without bargaining.
79KCwok324M.summary: Starting from the cupbearer whom Shaytan made forget Yusuf for some seven to nine years, he warns against a conditional relationship with Allah that expects every hardship to be followed by worldly ease. The Quran says ease comes with hardship, not necessarily after it, and everyone ends in the hardship of death with no ease after it in this world. Phrases like 'Allah has a plan for me, it will all work out' are foreign to Islam; sometimes a calamity is the result of our own deeds, yet in decades of work he has rarely heard anyone admit it. Islam promises a good life and the Hereafter, not wealth or health, and it guarantees trials. Yusuf took the means available, then accepted Allah's decree, as did companions like Imran ibn Husayn and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. He then explains the king's dream, the courtiers' dismissal of it as jumbled dreams, and the cupbearer's self-serving recall. Most striking is that Yusuf neither rebuked the man nor bargained for release; because the dream concerned whole populations, he gave not only the interpretation but a complete economic plan of planting, storing grain in the ear and rationing, which saved Egypt and its neighbours.

outline.heading: Shaytan made the cupbearer forget
outline.gist: Absorbed in worldly pleasures, he put Yusuf's request aside, as people do with favours asked of them.

outline.heading: Some years in prison
outline.gist: Bid' means three to nine; scholars favour seven to nine years of patient da'wah in prison.

outline.heading: Ease comes with hardship, not necessarily after it
outline.gist: Pray for relief and think well of Allah, but faith cannot be conditional on worldly relief.

outline.heading: The final hardship with no ease after it
outline.gist: Everyone faces the agony of death; ease awaits only in the Hereafter for those who did well.

outline.heading: A conditional relationship with Allah
outline.gist: Demanding that every trial be followed by gain risks disbelief.

outline.heading: 'Allah has a plan for me'
outline.gist: Such phrases are borrowed from other faiths; what does 'it will all work out' even mean?

outline.heading: Because of what your hands sent forth
outline.gist: A calamity may be a wake-up call caused by our own failings.

outline.heading: Self-accountability has run dry
outline.gist: In 22 years no one has told him a trial was his own fault; the jars of muhasabah are empty.

outline.heading: Worshipping Allah on an edge
outline.gist: Content when good comes, turning away when tested; ask to be servants of ihsan, not of testing.

outline.heading: Honour and humiliation are both tests
outline.gist: Life has ups and downs and no order is guaranteed; the righteous mostly lived in trial.

outline.heading: Imran ibn Husayn and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas
outline.gist: Thirty years of illness and blindness, yet content and not praying for their own relief.

outline.heading: Islam offers no worldly guarantees
outline.gist: It promises a good life of contentment and the true life of the Hereafter, not wealth or fame.

outline.heading: The one guarantee is trial
outline.gist: People will be tested; some treat people's harm like Allah's punishment and give up.

outline.heading: Yusuf's chain of trials
outline.gist: Separated from his mother and father, betrayed, sold, slandered and imprisoned through his twenties.

outline.heading: Patient and content while wanting release
outline.gist: Not happy in prison, but pleased with Allah and still seeking a way out.

outline.heading: Not every story ends well in this world
outline.gist: Zakariyya and Yahya were killed; some prophets come on the Day with no followers.

outline.heading: Hoping versus expecting
outline.gist: Ask Allah and hope; if it comes be grateful, if not be patient and review yourself.

outline.heading: Muhasabah without a filter
outline.gist: He wishes he could tell people plainly what their problem is, as one should with oneself.

outline.heading: Honesty with yourself brings peace
outline.gist: Use the open window for good while it lasts, and praise Allah when it closes.

outline.heading: Religions of false promises
outline.gist: Some offer that everything will work out; Islam says life is a test in both good and bad.

outline.heading: Prophets tested with wealth and with poverty
outline.gist: Those given kingdoms are said to enter Paradise after those who lived in hardship.

outline.heading: Take the means, then accept
outline.gist: Yusuf did what he could through the cupbearer; illness and family problems often cannot be changed.

outline.heading: Stay with Yusuf in prison
outline.gist: Do not rush to the happy ending; Yusuf found ease within hardship, which is more than patience.

outline.heading: Interlude
The king's recurring dream
outline.gist: A Hyksos king troubled by a repeated dream tells his court.

outline.heading: Seven fat cows eaten by seven lean
outline.gist: Cows symbolised abundance in ancient Egypt; lean cows devouring fat ones is unnatural.

outline.heading: Green ears and dry ones
outline.gist: Wheat symbolised rain and the land's bounty.

outline.heading: Unsown wheat and repeated dreams
outline.gist: Wheat that grows without sowing carries no zakat; true dreams tend to repeat.

outline.heading: Jumbled dreams
outline.gist: Dighth is a handful of grass pulled up at random; the courtiers dismiss the dream.

outline.heading: Dreams after a heavy dinner
outline.gist: Not every dream needs interpreting; a meaning is sought when a dream recurs.

outline.heading: The court admits it has no knowledge
outline.gist: No one could help the king, and the matter became the talk of the kingdom.

outline.heading: Iddakara: remembering that takes effect
outline.gist: The ifta'al form indicates the effect of remembering is realised.

outline.heading: 'Easy for remembrance' is about application
outline.gist: The verse in Al-Qamar is about acting on the Quran, not memorising it; some great scholars were not huffaz.

outline.heading: After an ummah: time and people
outline.gist: Ummah means both a span of time and people; he recalled once the matter became public.

outline.heading: 'I will inform you': the cupbearer's ego
outline.gist: The emphatic 'I' shows he wanted credit.

outline.heading: Yusuf, O truthful one
outline.gist: The cupbearer returns after a decade and asks for the interpretation.

outline.heading: A grammatical note on the two wordings
outline.gist: The case of 'seven' differs between the king's words and the cupbearer's.

outline.heading: When was Yusuf sent as a prophet?
outline.gist: Unknown; he will give his view at the end of the story.

outline.heading: The siddiq is a step below prophethood
outline.gist: Only revelation separates a siddiq from a prophet, as with Maryam and Abu Bakr.

outline.heading: Envy as a reason he forgot
outline.gist: People resent those who show complete character.

outline.heading: How Shaytan makes one forget
outline.gist: Shaytan needs fertile ground; he found Adam's fear of death and dislike of servitude.

outline.heading: Al-Razi: the entry was envy
outline.gist: He set it aside until it served him to remember.

outline.heading: 'Perhaps' twice: interpretation is probable, not certain
outline.gist: Dream interpretation is not an exact science, hence 'thought' in verse 42.

outline.heading: What we would have said
outline.gist: Nine years without a word, and now you come when you need me.

outline.heading: No reproach, no condition, no da'wah first
outline.gist: Yusuf could have bargained for release or made faith a condition, yet he answered at once.

outline.heading: Why: the dream concerned whole populations
outline.gist: Thousands would die if preparation did not start that day.

outline.heading: Caring for those who wronged him
outline.gist: The Aziz, his wife, his brothers, the caravan and Egypt's people, yet he cared for them; this is prophetic character.

outline.heading: Egypt as the hub of the world
outline.gist: Its ruin would have cut trade routes to the Hijaz, Sham, North Africa and Europe, so there was no time to negotiate.

outline.heading: Interlude
Sow seven years in succession, store in the ear
outline.gist: A full economic plan: continuous planting, grain kept in the ear to preserve it, eating only what is needed.

outline.heading: Seven hard years consume the stores
outline.gist: They will eat what was stored except a little kept in reserve.

outline.heading: A year of relief and pressing
outline.gist: Rain returns and people press milk and fruit again.

outline.heading: How he inferred the year of relief
outline.gist: Seven by seven means the cycle ends; wheat and cows signal rain and milk returning.

outline.heading: People came from every land
outline.gist: Famine was general; Yusuf's brothers came from far away for grain.

outline.heading: Strict rationing per family
outline.gist: Rations per head and trading goods to stretch reserves explain the demand for the tenth brother.

outline.heading: A wronged prisoner saved humanity
outline.gist: Precise rationing was needed to last seven years, and an oppressed prisoner made it possible.

outline.heading: Outro

0hNisug1JJI.title: Deeds Rendered Unacceptable #3: Mountains of Good Deeds Turned to Dust
0hNisug1JJI.one_line: The hadith of Thawban about people whose mountains of good deeds become scattered dust because they violate Allah's limits in private.
0hNisug1JJI.summary: Continuing his series on deeds that lose their reward, he narrates the hadith of Thawban, the freed slave of the Prophet, recorded by Ibn Majah with a sound chain. He first explains why Thawban is called 'mawla' of the Prophet: a freed slave without a tribe attached himself to a figure, since in Islam one cannot claim to be someone's son. Then the hadith: some people of this ummah will come on the Day of Resurrection with good deeds like the white mountains of Tihamah, and Allah will make them scattered dust. He calls this a nightmare statement, because we all hope our good outweighs our bad on the scale. Thawban asked the Prophet to describe them so they would not become such people unknowingly. The Prophet said they are from among you, of your own skin, and take from the night as you do, but when they are alone with what Allah has forbidden, they violate it. He draws the lesson that private sin, committed whenever no one whose judgment we care about is watching, is what wipes out these deeds. The remedy is to cultivate in the heart a living awareness that Allah sees us when no one else does, and to care about His gaze more than people's.

full.full_ar: يروي الإمام ابن ماجه في سننه (4245) قال: حدثنا عيسى بن يونس الرملي، حدثنا عقبة بن علقمة بن حديج المعافري، عن أرطاة بن المنذر، عن أبي عامر الألهاني، عن ثوبان، عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: «لأعلمن أقواما من أمتي يأتون يوم القيامة بحسنات أمثال جبال تهامة بيضا، فيجعلها الله عز وجل هباء منثورا». قال ثوبان: يا رسول الله صفهم لنا، جلّهم لنا، أن لا نكون منهم ونحن لا نعلم. قال: «أما إنهم إخوانكم ومن جلدتكم، ويأخذون من الليل كما تأخذون، ولكنهم أقوام إذا خلوا بمحارم الله انتهكوها».
full.full_en: Imam Ibn Majah narrates in his Sunan (4245): 'Isa ibn Yunus al-Ramli narrated to us from 'Uqbah ibn 'Alqamah ibn Hudayj al-Ma'afiri, from Artat ibn al-Mundhir, from Abu 'Amir al-Alhani, from Thawban, that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "I certainly know people of my ummah who will come on the Day of Resurrection with good deeds like the mountains of Tihamah, white, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic will make them scattered dust." Thawban said: "O Messenger of Allah, describe them to us, make them clear to us, so that we do not become of them without knowing." He said: "They are your brothers, of your own skin, and they take of the night as you take, but they are people who, when alone with what Allah has made sacred, violate it."

ZjgaWCHAMe0.title: Descriptions of the Prophet, Part 10: His Names
ZjgaWCHAMe0.one_line: The Prophet's names as descriptions: Muhammad and Ahmad tied to praise and gratitude, the obliterator, gatherer and final prophet, and his austere food.
ZjgaWCHAMe0.summary: Reading chapter 51 of al-Tirmidhi's Shama'il on the names of the Prophet, he explains that these names are descriptions, the ways Allah describes him to his followers, not legal names. Muhammad, the name used in his lifetime, and Ahmad, the name in the scripture given to Jesus, are both bound up with praise and gratitude: Ahmad is the one who praised Allah most, and Muhammad the one most praised by people for his deeds. He is the obliterator by whom Allah removes disbelief, the gatherer at whose feet mankind will gather on the Day of Judgment as he intercedes, and the final one after whom there is no prophet. That last name means we live in a unique time with no prophets or prophecies to come; what remains is what each person chooses to accept and understand. He then reads a narration on the Prophet's lifestyle in which a companion reminds people that they eat and drink freely, while the Prophet at times could not find even the lowest-grade dates to fill his stomach. The point he draws is simple: be grateful for what you have and carry out your duties.

a8YE_PeCbPA.title: Descriptions of the Prophet, Part 9: Never Vulgar, Never Vengeful
a8YE_PeCbPA.one_line: Two narrations from Aisha: the Prophet was never obscene or loud, never repaid evil with evil, never avenged himself, and chose the easier path.
a8YE_PeCbPA.summary: He reads two narrations from Aisha in al-Tirmidhi's Shama'il on the Prophet's general character. In the first, she says he was neither obscene nor did he seek obscenity, was not loud in the markets, and did not repay a bad deed with a bad deed but pardoned and overlooked. He explains that fahsh refers specifically to sexual indecency and crude speech about it, and notes that men in particular fall into it quickly when given the chance. He stresses the weight of a wife's testimony, since a wife knows her husband's true character, and she said this after his death. In the second, Aisha says she never saw him take revenge for a wrong done to him personally unless one of Allah's limits was violated, in which case he was the angriest of them, and that whenever he was given a choice between two matters he chose the easier as long as it was not sinful. He points out how contrary this is to our instinct: an injustice against ourselves ruins our week while one against others barely touches us. He adds that there is no merit in making life artificially difficult; the Prophet chose ease, except where righteousness required the harder path.

iVSuT5nHWQg.title: Knowledge Is Taken by the Death of Scholars
iVSuT5nHWQg.one_line: A hadith on knowledge leaving with its scholars, applied to influencers and AI chatbots as today's sources of religious answers.
iVSuT5nHWQg.summary: The speaker reads the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that Allah does not remove knowledge by snatching it from people but by taking the scholars, until people take ignorant leaders who give rulings without knowledge, go astray and lead others astray. He applies it to the present: Muslims, and young people especially, are squeezed between two poles. On one side are online influencers who speak about Islam with the loudest voices and largest followings and treat disagreement like a rap feud; on the other are AI chatbots that people now ask their religious questions. He argues that parents and adults must teach the epistemological basis of the faith: what counts as truth in the religion, where it comes from and where it can be learned. In a city like London there is no shortage of qualified teachers, some of them sitting in the congregation, so there is no need to turn to chatbots or YouTubers. He warns that a time may come when scholars are truly scarce, and those who abandon the scholars they have now hardly deserve to reach that day. He closes by asking people to return to sources and to the scholars among them.

I1jRPt7Qjhw.title: Descriptions of the Prophet #8: His Humility
I1jRPt7Qjhw.one_line: From the Shama'il chapter on humility: the Prophet visited the sick, rode donkeys, ate humble food and died with his armour pawned.
I1jRPt7Qjhw.summary: He opens the Shama'il chapter on the Prophet's humility by calling humility the master of all character traits, warning that false humility is among the worst things a person can have, and that its absence leaves arrogance, vanity, envy and showing off. The Prophet was naturally humble: secure in his worth, untroubled by others' wealth or popularity, focused on his mission. When people say they follow the sunnah, this should be the first thing they think of, before appearance. Through Anas, who lived with him from childhood and saw him with a child's sharp eye, he lists what the Prophet did even as head of state in Madinah: visiting the sick, attending funerals, riding a donkey with palm-fibre reins, accepting a slave's invitation to simple food. He admits he no longer visits the sick as he once did. The Prophet accepted a meal of barley bread and stale fat so no one would think him above it, and the Umar story shows how his successors carried the same expectation. He died with his armour pawned to a Jewish neighbour after borrowing to help someone, because he chose a life of zuhd. He asks the audience to love and adopt this trait.

full.full_ar: يروي الإمام الترمذي في الشمائل المحمدية (331) قال: حَدَّثَنَا عَلِيُّ بْنُ حُجْرٍ، قَالَ: حَدَّثَنَا عَلِيُّ بْنُ مُسْهِرٍ، عَنْ مُسْلِمٍ الأَعْوَرِ، عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ، قال: «كَانَ رَسُولُ اللهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَعُودُ الْمَرِيضَ، وَيَشْهَدُ الْجَنَائِزَ، وَيَرْكَبُ الْحِمَارَ، وَيُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ الْعَبْدِ، وَكَانَ يَوْمَ بَنِي قُرَيْظَةَ عَلَى حِمَارٍ مَخْطُومٍ بِحَبْلٍ مِنْ لِيفٍ، وَعَلَيْهِ إِكَافٌ مِنْ لِيفٍ»
full.full_en: Imam al-Tirmidhi narrates in al-Shama'il al-Muhammadiyyah (331): Ali ibn Hujr narrated to us from Ali ibn Mushir, from Muslim al-A'war, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) used to visit the sick, attend funerals, ride a donkey and accept the invitation of a slave. On the day of Banu Qurayzah he was on a donkey bridled with a rope of palm fibre, with a saddle of palm fibre."
full.isnad_ar: حَدَّثَنَا عَلِيُّ بْنُ حُجْرٍ، قَالَ: حَدَّثَنَا عَلِيُّ بْنُ مُسْهِرٍ، عَنْ مُسْلِمٍ الأَعْوَرِ، عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ
full.isnad_en: Ali ibn Hujr, from Ali ibn Mushir, from Muslim al-A'war, from Anas ibn Malik.
full.ar_block: يروي الإمام الترمذي في الشمائل المحمدية، بسند ضعيف، عن أنس بن مالك رضي الله عنه قال: «كَانَ رَسُولُ اللهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَعُودُ الْمَرِيضَ، وَيَشْهَدُ الْجَنَائِزَ، وَيَرْكَبُ الْحِمَارَ، وَيُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ الْعَبْدِ، وَكَانَ يَوْمَ بَنِي قُرَيْظَةَ عَلَى حِمَارٍ مَخْطُومٍ بِحَبْلٍ مِنْ لِيفٍ، وَعَلَيْهِ إِكَافٌ مِنْ لِيفٍ»

On the day of Banu Qurayzah he was on a donkey bridled with a rope of palm fibre, with a saddle of palm fibre."

full.full_ar: يروي الإمام الترمذي في الشمائل المحمدية (332) قال: حَدَّثَنَا وَاصِلُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الأَعْلَى الْكُوفِيُّ، قَالَ: حَدَّثَنَا مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ فُضَيْلٍ، عَنِ الأَعْمَشِ، عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ، قال: «كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم يُدْعَى إِلَى خُبْزِ الشَّعِيرِ، وَالإِهَالَةِ السَّنِخَةِ، فَيُجِيبُ، وَلَقَدْ كَانَ لَهُ دِرْعٌ عِنْدَ يَهُودِيٍّ، فَمَا وَجَدَ مَا يَفُكُّهَا حَتَّى مَاتَ»

He had a coat of armour held by a Jewish man, and he did not find the means to redeem it until he died."

full.full_en: Imam al-Bukhari narrates in his Sahih (2916): Muhammad ibn Kathir narrated to us from Sufyan (al-Thawri), from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i), from al-Aswad (ibn Yazid), from Aisha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) died while his armour was pawned to a Jewish man for thirty sa' of barley."

zbr5nUX_ZRw.title: Do Not Be an Imma'ah
zbr5nUX_ZRw.one_line: Explains the Tirmidhi hadith forbidding being a yes-man who does good or bad only as the crowd does.
zbr5nUX_ZRw.summary: He comments on the hadith of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman in Tirmidhi's Jami', graded hasan: do not be an imma'ah, saying that if people do well you will do well and if they do wrong you will do wrong; rather settle yourselves so that you do well when people do well and do not do wrong when they do wrong. He starts from the common error of individuals and communities who simply continue with the norm because it is easier, needs no justification and involves no struggle. He explains that imma'ah describes someone without the capacity to make his own decisions, who does whatever pleases those around him. Everyone passes through a people-pleasing phase, he says, and the Prophet asks us not to remain in it. He contrasts this with the pre-Islamic poet who boasted that he was only a man of his tribe, straying when it strayed and guided when it was guided. The prophetic word 'wattinu' means to settle and anchor yourself: your good conduct should not be conditional on how others behave but rest on what you believe and understand, so you break those chains and do not let waves of social corruption carry you.

KozXqKSMIHI.title: Tafseer of Surat 'Abasa, Part 3 (80:33-42) and the Opening of At-Takwir
KozXqKSMIHI.one_line: Gratitude as the core ethic of 'Abasa, the deafening blast and fleeing from family, then freedom of choice and the opening scenes of At-Takwir.
KozXqKSMIHI.summary: He closes 'Abasa by returning to the food verses as a lesson in gratitude. Gratitude is not contentment with mediocrity or acceptance of injustice; it is the feeling that you owe something for what you never earned, and it brings inner peace and motivates action. The Quran points to blessings common to all humans, not personal achievements, and grateful people are calmer and decide better. He tells the story of 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, who lost a leg and a son in one journey and thanked Allah for what remained. The deafening blast mirrors the voluntary deafness of those who ignore reminders. On that day a person flees from brother, parents, spouse and children; he pictures families holding together while one member, who lived ungratefully, runs alone. Faces will be either bright or covered in dust, and he defines fujur as discarding one's ethical restraint and kufr here as ingratitude. Islam is first a moral code, and prayer is only as strong as the life lived outside it. Introducing the next cluster of surahs on free choice, he criticises parents who bail children out and deprive them of accountability, explains that Islam means surrendering one's will only to Allah, and begins At-Takwir, urging listeners to picture the cosmic collapse it describes rather than outsourcing imagination to screens.

5PysgG55msY.title: Descriptions of the Prophet, Part 11: His Death
5PysgG55msY.one_line: Narrations from al-Tirmidhi's Shama'il on the Prophet's final illness and death, and what his passing meant to those around him.
5PysgG55msY.summary: Reaching the chapter on the Prophet's death in al-Tirmidhi's Shama'il, he reads a few narrations rather than the whole chapter. Aisha describes the Prophet at the point of death dipping his hand in a cup of water, wiping his face and asking Allah to help him through the agonies of death. He reflects that death is never easy or something to look forward to, yet it will reach everyone present within a century and the Prophet knew it was coming and did not fight it. Prophets are tested more severely than others, which is why his final illness was so heavy. Anas recalls that the day the Prophet entered Madinah everything lit up, and the day he died everything went dark; before they had even dusted off their hands from his burial they no longer recognised their own hearts. He dwells on the emptiness the companions felt, as if they no longer knew how to live. Fatimah's cry at her father's distress and his answer that there would be no distress for him after that day lead to the meeting on the Day of Resurrection, when every hardship and injustice comes full circle. He closes by reminding them that the book exists so they can study and follow the Prophet's character.

full.full_en: Imam al-Tirmidhi narrates in his Jami' (978): Qutaybah narrated to us from al-Layth, from Ibn al-Had, from Musa ibn Sarjis, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from 'A'ishah that she said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) while he was dying, with a cup of water beside him. He would put his hand into the cup, then wipe his face with the water, then say: O Allah, help me through the throes of death (or: the agonies of death)."

full.en_block: Imam al-Tirmidhi narrates in his Jami', with a weak chain, from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that she said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) while he was dying, with a cup of water beside him. He would put his hand into the cup, then wipe his face with the water, then say: O Allah, help me through the throes of death (or: the agonies of death)."
full.grade: Weak (da'if) in this wording. Tirmidhi: gharib. Da'if per Ahmad Shakir, al-Albani and Shu'ayb al-Arna'ut (on Ibn Majah 1623); Zubair 'Ali Za'i: isnad hasan. The weak point is Musa ibn Sarjis, whose reliability is unknown (mastur).
full.note: The sheikh cited al-Shama'il; the same route is in Tirmidhi 978 and Ibn Majah 1623. The authentic version is Bukhari 6510/4449 from 'A'ishah: he dipped his hands in water, wiped his face and said «لا إله إلا الله، إن للموت سكرات», then «في الرفيق الأعلى». The dua 'help me through the agonies of death' itself is only in the weak route.

full.full_ar: يروي الإمام ابن ماجه في سننه (4024) قال: حَدَّثَنَا عَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنُ إِبْرَاهِيمَ، حَدَّثَنَا ابْنُ أَبِي فُدَيْكٍ، حَدَّثَنِي هِشَامُ بْنُ سَعْدٍ، عَنْ زَيْدِ بْنِ أَسْلَمَ، عَنْ عَطَاءِ بْنِ يَسَارٍ، عَنْ أَبِي سَعِيدٍ الْخُدْرِيِّ، قال: «دَخَلْتُ عَلَى النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَهُوَ يُوعَكُ فَوَضَعْتُ يَدِي عَلَيْهِ فَوَجَدْتُ حَرَّهُ بَيْنَ يَدَىَّ فَوْقَ اللِّحَافِ فَقُلْتُ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ مَا أَشَدَّهَا عَلَيْكَ قَالَ “إِنَّا كَذَلِكَ يُضَعَّفُ لَنَا الْبَلاَءُ وَيُضَعَّفُ لَنَا الأَجْرُ”. قُلْتُ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ أَىُّ النَّاسِ أَشَدُّ بَلاَءً قَالَ “الأَنْبِيَاءُ”. قُلْتُ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ثُمَّ مَنْ قَالَ “ثُمَّ الصَّالِحُونَ إِنْ كَانَ أَحَدُهُمْ لَيُبْتَلَى بِالْفَقْرِ حَتَّى مَا يَجِدُ أَحَدُهُمْ إِلاَّ الْعَبَاءَةَ يُحَوِّيهَا وَإِنْ كَانَ أَحَدُهُمْ لَيَفْرَحُ بِالْبَلاَءِ كَمَا يَفْرَحُ أَحَدُكُمْ بِالرَّخَاءِ”»

I put my hand on him and felt its heat on my hands from above the blanket. I said: O Messenger of Allah, how severe it is on you! He said: 'That is how we are: the trial is doubled for us, and the reward is doubled for us.' I said: O Messenger of Allah, which people are tested most severely? He said: 'The prophets.' I said: O Messenger of Allah, then who? He said: 'Then the righteous. One of them would be tested with poverty until he could find nothing but a cloak to wrap around himself, and one of them would rejoice at trial as one of you rejoices at ease.'"

full.note: The gist joins two narrations. This one (Abu Sa'id) carries both points: the trial is doubled for us, and the prophets are tested most. The 'fever like two men' wording is Ibn Mas'ud's narration in Sahih al-Bukhari 5648 (and Muslim 2571), where the Prophet says: إني أوعك كما يوعك رجلان منكم, and agrees it means a double reward.

hadith.gist: Anas: the day the Prophet entered Madinah everything in it lit up, and the day he died everything darkened; we had not dusted off our hands from his burial before we no longer recognised our hearts.

full.full_ar: يروي الإمام الترمذي في جامعه (3618) قال: حَدَّثَنَا بِشْرُ بْنُ هِلاَلٍ الصَّوَّافُ الْبَصْرِيُّ، حَدَّثَنَا جَعْفَرُ بْنُ سُلَيْمَانَ الضُّبَعِيُّ، عَنْ ثَابِتٍ، عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ، قال: «لَمَّا كَانَ الْيَوْمُ الَّذِي دَخَلَ فِيهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم الْمَدِينَةَ أَضَاءَ مِنْهَا كُلُّ شَيْءٍ فَلَمَّا كَانَ الْيَوْمُ الَّذِي مَاتَ فِيهِ أَظْلَمَ مِنْهَا كُلُّ شَيْءٍ وَمَا نَفَضْنَا عَنْ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم الأَيْدِي وَإِنَّا لَفِي دَفْنِهِ حَتَّى أَنْكَرْنَا قُلُوبَنَا»
full.full_en: Imam al-Tirmidhi narrates in his Jami' (3618): Bishr ibn Hilal al-Sawwaf al-Basri narrated to us from Ja'far ibn Sulayman al-Duba'i, from Thabit (al-Bunani), from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "On the day the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) entered Madinah, everything in it was lit up, and on the day he died, everything in it went dark. And we had not yet dusted off our hands from the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him), while we were still burying him, before we no longer recognised our own hearts."
full.isnad_ar: حَدَّثَنَا بِشْرُ بْنُ هِلاَلٍ الصَّوَّافُ الْبَصْرِيُّ، حَدَّثَنَا جَعْفَرُ بْنُ سُلَيْمَانَ الضُّبَعِيُّ، عَنْ ثَابِتٍ، عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ

And we had not yet dusted off our hands from the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him), while we were still burying him, before we no longer recognised our own hearts."
full.grade: Al-Tirmidhi: gharib sahih. Sahih per Ahmad Shakir, al-Albani and Bashar Awwad Ma'ruf. Zubair Ali Za'i: isnad hasan (Ja'far ibn Sulayman al-Duba'i is saduq, noted for Shi'i leanings). Same chain and wording also in Ibn Majah 1631 (sahih per al-Albani and al-Arna'ut).

hadith.gist: Fatimah cried out at her father's distress; he said there would be no distress for your father after today, and the meeting is on the Day of Resurrection.

full.full_ar: يروي الإمام ابن ماجه في سننه (1629) قال: حَدَّثَنَا نَصْرُ بْنُ عَلِيٍّ، حَدَّثَنَا عَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ الزُّبَيْرِ أَبُو الزُّبَيْرِ، حَدَّثَنَا ثَابِتٌ الْبُنَانِيُّ، عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ، قال: «لَمَّا وَجَدَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم مِنْ كَرْبِ الْمَوْتِ مَا وَجَدَ قَالَتْ فَاطِمَةُ وَاكَرْبَ أَبَتَاهْ. فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم “لاَ كَرْبَ عَلَى أَبِيكِ بَعْدَ الْيَوْمِ إِنَّهُ قَدْ حَضَرَ مِنْ أَبِيكِ مَا لَيْسَ بِتَارِكٍ مِنْهُ أَحَدًا الْمُوَافَاةُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ”»
full.full_en: Imam Ibn Majah narrates in his Sunan (1629): Nasr ibn Ali narrated to us from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr Abu al-Zubayr (al-Bahili), from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) felt the agony of death that he felt, Fatimah said: 'Oh, the distress of my father!' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no distress for your father after today. There has come to your father that from which no one is spared, and the meeting is on the Day of Resurrection.'"

full.en_block: Imam Ibn Majah narrates in his Sunan, with a hasan chain, that Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "When the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) felt the agony of death that he felt, Fatimah said: 'Oh, the distress of my father!' full.grade: Hasan sahih per al-Albani and Abd al-Baqi; hasan per Shu'ayb al-Arna'ut (Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr al-Bahili is only saduq); sahih per Zubair Ali Za'i. The core of the story is in Sahih al-Bukhari 4462 (Thabit from Anas).

17:36.ar: وَلَا تَقۡفُ مَا لَيۡسَ لَكَ بِهِۦ عِلۡمٌۚ إِنَّ ٱلسَّمۡعَ وَٱلۡبَصَرَ وَٱلۡفُؤَادَ كُلُّ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ كَانَ عَنۡهُ مَسۡـُٔولࣰ ا
17:36.en: (O man), follow not that whereof thou hast no knowledge. Lo! the hearing and the sight and the heart - of each of these it will be asked

4:62.ar: فَكَيۡفَ إِذَآ أَصَٰبَتۡهُم مُّصِيبَةُۢ بِمَا قَدَّمَتۡ أَيۡدِيهِمۡ ثُمَّ جَآءُوكَ يَحۡلِفُونَ بِٱللَّهِ إِنۡ أَرَدۡنَآ إِلَّآ إِحۡسَٰنࣰ ا وَتَوۡفِيقًا
4:62.en: How would it be if a misfortune smote them because of that which their own hands have sent before (them)? Then would they come unto thee, swearing by Allah that they were seeking naught but harmony and kindness

9:107.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّخَذُواْ مَسۡجِدࣰ ا ضِرَارࣰ ا وَكُفۡرࣰ ا وَتَفۡرِيقَۢا بَيۡنَ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ وَإِرۡصَادࣰ ا لِّمَنۡ حَارَبَ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۥ مِن قَبۡلُۚ وَلَيَحۡلِفُنَّ إِنۡ أَرَدۡنَآ إِلَّا ٱلۡحُسۡنَىٰۖ وَٱللَّهُ يَشۡهَدُ إِنَّهُمۡ لَكَٰذِبُونَ
9:107.en: And as for those who chose a place of worship out of opposition and disbelief, and in order to cause dissent among the believers, and as an outpost for those who warred against Allah and His messenger aforetime, they will surely swear: We purposed naught save good. Allah beareth witness that they verily are liars

D8fuqzynK5Y.title: Essentials and Pet Peeves: Good Intentions Are Not Enough
D8fuqzynK5Y.one_line: Good intentions do not excuse incompetence, justify corrupt means, or remove accountability for harm; take on only what you are qualified for.
D8fuqzynK5Y.summary: He states the pet peeve in one sentence and repeats it: good intentions do not excuse incompetence, do not justify corrupt means, and do not remove accountability when harm is caused. He compares it to culpable negligence, and to a child protesting that he did not mean to. Corrupt means are never excusable, since Allah has no interest in what is achieved through them. He cites the verse forbidding pursuit of what one has no knowledge of, the hadith of an army swallowed by the earth and resurrected according to intentions, and the hadith that whoever practises medicine without knowledge is liable. He criticises people who give marital, mental health or medical advice without training, such as telling a person with schizophrenia that he has a jinn, and those who run institutions and mosques with no experience; entrusting matters to the unqualified is a sign of the Hour. The hypocrites who swore they intended only good, and the builders of the harmful mosque, show that intentions do not undo harm. Imam Ahmad chose the strong sinner over the weak pious commander, and the Prophet told Abu Dharr he would not appoint him over even two people. He asks each person to judge their own competence before taking on responsibility.

outline.heading: Opening
Do not pursue what you have no knowledge of
outline.gist: Hearing, sight and heart will all be questioned.

outline.heading: Interlude
The pet peeve in one sentence
outline.gist: Good intentions don't excuse incompetence, justify corrupt means or remove accountability; the law calls it culpable negligence.

outline.heading: 'I didn't mean to': teaching children
outline.gist: Did you assess the risk, were you trained, did you ask permission? Meaning well does not undo negligence.

outline.heading: Corrupt means are never excusable
outline.gist: Allah has no interest in anything achieved through corrupt means.

outline.heading: Were you competent enough to act?
outline.gist: Taking on what you do not understand means answering for your hearing, sight and heart.

outline.heading: Meaning well does not make critics wrong
outline.gist: 'I sacrificed so much' does not mean those who criticise the outcome are bad.

outline.heading: Intentions are for Allah; outcomes are judged here
outline.gist: Allah may forgive the well-meaning, as the army swallowed by the earth is resurrected on its intentions, but intentions do not cover incompetence.

outline.heading: Practising medicine without knowledge makes you liable
outline.gist: The hadith in Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i applied to anyone offering expertise they lack.

outline.heading: Untrained advice that harms
outline.gist: Marital, mental health and medical advice from the unqualified, like telling a person with schizophrenia he has a jinn.

outline.heading: Running institutions without experience
outline.gist: People run mosques and organisations and seek positions with no training; he assumes good intentions, but they do not help.

outline.heading: Entrusting matters to the unqualified: a sign of the Hour
outline.gist: The Prophet saw placing affairs in the wrong hands as a sign of the end.

outline.heading: 'We intended only good': the hypocrites' oath
outline.gist: When disaster came from their choices they swore they meant only good; the Quran treats this severely.

outline.heading: 'I got the job done' by corrupt means
outline.gist: There is no barakah in results reached the wrong way; that is why we ask daily for the straight path.

outline.heading: Harming others on the way to prayer
outline.gist: Dangerous driving or blocking others to reach the masjid is not excused by a good goal.

outline.heading: Epistemic humility
outline.gist: Speaking on what we do not understand and making untrained decisions leaves us accountable; youth must learn intentions are not enough.

outline.heading: Opening
Good intention does not replace qualification
outline.gist: An ignorant person who causes harm is liable; his intention is between him and Allah.

outline.heading: Learn, train and consult before acting
outline.gist: Even the qualified work with advisers; volunteers often act alone without asking whether they help or harm.

outline.heading: A goal reached through injustice
outline.gist: Worse still is achieving the goal through wrongs and violations; Allah does not bless it.

outline.heading: The harmful mosque
outline.gist: Its builders swore they intended good, yet it divided the believers.

outline.heading: How did that person get there?
outline.gist: Much of what is wrong with the world is unqualified people in positions; he prefers the competent over the merely well-meaning.

outline.heading: Imam Ahmad: the strong sinner or the weak pious?
outline.gist: The pious man's piety benefits himself and his weakness harms the people; the strong sinner's strength serves the people.

outline.heading: Not a revolution: assess yourself
outline.gist: He is not asking people to judge others but to examine their own competence before taking responsibility.

outline.heading: Abu Dharr, an early supporter

-ioApnLBaek.title: Deeds Rendered Unacceptable, Part 1: Speaking on Allah's Behalf
-ioApnLBaek.one_line: The hadith of the man who swore Allah would not forgive someone: never speak for Allah, and guard deeds against losing their value.
-ioApnLBaek.summary: He begins a short series of hadith on deeds that Allah rejects, starting with the narration of a man who swore that Allah would not forgive a certain sinner, and Allah replied that He had forgiven that man and voided the deeds of the one who swore. He draws two layers from it. First, people may decide for themselves whether to forgive someone who wronged them; refusing to forgive is permitted though not recommended, especially for something as hard to repair as betrayal. But declaring that Allah will not forgive someone is a different matter entirely: it presumes to speak for Allah. He recalls how al-Hajjaj, as he was dying, asked Allah to forgive him despite everyone saying He never would, and how a great scholar of the time feared that this plea might be answered. Second, deeds can be grayed out and lose all worth, through outward mistakes in how they are performed or inward failures of intention, goal and etiquette. Since the quality of our deeds is never high, he asks people to spend their lives improving them and to pray constantly that Allah accepts them, lest a lifetime of effort turn out to be wasted.

full.full_ar: يروي الإمام مسلم في صحيحه (2621) قال: حدثنا سويد بن سعيد، عن معتمر بن سليمان، عن أبيه، حدثنا أبو عمران الجوني، عن جندب، أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حدّث: «أن رجلا قال: والله لا يغفر الله لفلان، وإن الله تعالى قال: من ذا الذي يتألّى عليّ أن لا أغفر لفلان، فإني قد غفرت لفلان وأحبطت عملك» أو كما قال.
full.full_en: Imam Muslim narrates in his Sahih (2621): Suwayd ibn Sa'id narrated to us from Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman, from his father (Sulayman al-Taymi), from Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, from Jundub (ibn 'Abdillah al-Bajali), that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) related: "A man said: By Allah, Allah will not forgive so-and-so. And Allah the Exalted said: Who is this who swears by Me that I will not forgive so-and-so? I have forgiven so-and-so and nullified your deeds" (or as he said).
full.isnad_ar: حدثنا سويد بن سعيد، عن معتمر بن سليمان، عن أبيه، حدثنا أبو عمران الجوني، عن جندب
full.isnad_en: Muslim from Suwayd ibn Sa'id, from Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman, from his father (Sulayman al-Taymi), from Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, from Jundub (ibn 'Abdillah al-Bajali)
full.ar_block: يروي الإمام مسلم في صحيحه، بسند صحيح، عن جندب بن عبد الله رضي الله عنه، أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حدّث: «أن رجلا قال: والله لا يغفر الله لفلان، وإن الله تعالى قال: من ذا الذي يتألّى عليّ أن لا أغفر لفلان، فإني قد غفرت لفلان وأحبطت عملك» أو كما قال.
full.en_block: Imam Muslim narrates in his Sahih, with an authentic chain, from Jundub ibn 'Abdillah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) related: "A man said: By Allah, Allah will not forgive so-and-so. And Allah the Exalted said: Who is this who swears by Me that I will not forgive so-and-so? I have forgiven so-and-so and nullified your deeds" (or as he said).
full.note: Suwayd ibn Sa'id is a contested narrator (truthful but accepted prompting after he went blind); Muslim's inclusion is accepted and the hadith is graded sahih. A fuller story version (two men of Bani Isra'il, one devout, one sinful) is in Abu Dawud 4901 from Abu Hurayrah.

12:37.en: He said: The food which ye are given (daily) shall not come unto you but I shall tell you the interpretation ere it cometh unto you. This is of that which my Lord hath taught me. Lo! I have forsaken the religion of folk who believe not in Allah and are disbelievers in the Hereafter

12:38.ar: وَٱتَّبَعۡتُ مِلَّةَ ءَابَآءِيٓ إِبۡرَٰهِيمَ وَإِسۡحَٰقَ وَيَعۡقُوبَۚ مَا كَانَ لَنَآ أَن نُّشۡرِكَ بِٱللَّهِ مِن شَيۡءࣲۚ ذَٰلِكَ مِن فَضۡلِ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡنَا وَعَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَ ٱلنَّاسِ لَا يَشۡكُرُونَ
12:38.en: And I have followed the religion of my fathers, Abraham and Isaac and Jacob. It never was for us to attribute aught as partner to Allah. This is of the bounty of Allah unto us (the seed of Abraham) and unto mankind; but most men give not thanks

12:39.ar: يَٰصَٰحِبَيِ ٱلسِّجۡنِ ءَأَرۡبَابࣱ مُّتَفَرِّقُونَ خَيۡرٌ أَمِ ٱللَّهُ ٱلۡوَٰحِدُ ٱلۡقَهَّارُ
12:39.en: O my fellow-prisoners! Are divers lords better, or Allah the One, Almighty

12:40.ar: مَا تَعۡبُدُونَ مِن دُونِهِۦٓ إِلَّآ أَسۡمَآءࣰ سَمَّيۡتُمُوهَآ أَنتُمۡ وَءَابَآؤُكُم مَّآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ بِهَا مِن سُلۡطَٰنٍۚ إِنِ ٱلۡحُكۡمُ إِلَّا لِلَّهِ أَمَرَ أَلَّا تَعۡبُدُوٓاْ إِلَّآ إِيَّاهُۚ ذَٰلِكَ ٱلدِّينُ ٱلۡقَيِّمُ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَ ٱلنَّاسِ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
12:40.en: Those whom ye worship beside Him are but names which ye have named, ye and your fathers. Allah hath revealed no sanction for them. The decision rests with Allah only, Who hath commanded you that ye worship none save Him. This is the right religion, but most men know not

12:41.ar: يَٰصَٰحِبَيِ ٱلسِّجۡنِ أَمَّآ أَحَدُكُمَا فَيَسۡقِي رَبَّهُۥ خَمۡرࣰ اۖ وَأَمَّا ٱلۡأٓخَرُ فَيُصۡلَبُ فَتَأۡكُلُ ٱلطَّيۡرُ مِن رَّأۡسِهِۦۚ قُضِيَ ٱلۡأَمۡرُ ٱلَّذِي فِيهِ تَسۡتَفۡتِيَانِ
12:41.en: O my two fellow-prisoners! As for one of you, he will pour out wine for his lord to drink; and as for the other, he will be crucified so that the birds will eat from his head. Thus is the case judged concerning which ye did inquire

12:42.ar: وَقَالَ لِلَّذِي ظَنَّ أَنَّهُۥ نَاجࣲ مِّنۡهُمَا ٱذۡكُرۡنِي عِندَ رَبِّكَ فَأَنسَىٰهُ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنُ ذِكۡرَ رَبِّهِۦ فَلَبِثَ فِي ٱلسِّجۡنِ بِضۡعَ سِنِينَ
12:42.en: And he said unto him of the twain who he knew would be released: Mention me in the presence of thy lord. But Satan caused him to forget to mention it to his lord, so he (Joseph) stayed in prison for some years

12:43.ar: وَقَالَ ٱلۡمَلِكُ إِنِّيٓ أَرَىٰ سَبۡعَ بَقَرَٰتࣲ سِمَانࣲ يَأۡكُلُهُنَّ سَبۡعٌ عِجَافࣱ وَسَبۡعَ سُنۢبُلَٰتٍ خُضۡرࣲ وَأُخَرَ يَابِسَٰتࣲۖ يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلۡمَلَأُ أَفۡتُونِي فِي رُءۡيَٰيَ إِن كُنتُمۡ لِلرُّءۡيَا تَعۡبُرُونَ
12:43.en: And the king said: Lo! I saw in a dream seven fat kine which seven lean were eating, and seven green ears of corn and other (seven) dry. O notables! Expound for me my vision, if ye can interpret dreams

39:29.ar: ضَرَبَ ٱللَّهُ مَثَلࣰ ا رَّجُلࣰ ا فِيهِ شُرَكَآءُ مُتَشَٰكِسُونَ وَرَجُلࣰ ا سَلَمࣰ ا لِّرَجُلٍ هَلۡ يَسۡتَوِيَانِ مَثَلًاۚ ٱلۡحَمۡدُ لِلَّهِۚ بَلۡ أَكۡثَرُهُمۡ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ

Condemn us not if we forget, or miss the mark! Our Lord! Lay not on us such a burden as thou didst lay on those before us! Our Lord! Impose not on us that which we have not the strength to bear! dahi0AJ7bCM.title: Arabic Tafsir of Surat Yusuf: Yusuf's Call in Prison and the King's Dream (12:37-43)
dahi0AJ7bCM.one_line: Yusuf invites his fellow prisoners to tawhid before interpreting their dreams; tawhid as fixed ethics and courage; his years in prison; the king's dream.
dahi0AJ7bCM.summary: He continues with Yusuf in prison. Before answering the two young men, Yusuf credits his knowledge to his Lord and explains that he left his captors' creed after examining it, following his forefathers' religion by conviction rather than inheritance. He then asks whether scattered lords are better than Allah, the One, the Subduer. He argues that tawhid is more than belief: a monotheistic society has fixed morals because they come from one source, while a society with many lords bends rules through bribes, connections and favours, a shirk in ethics that turns the shahadah into mere prestige. Idols are only names, images inflated by people, like a ribboned tree he remembers from Syria, Pharaoh, or modern rulers. A true monotheist fears only Allah, which is why tyrants promote a submissive religiosity; tawhid obliges caring about wrong even when one cannot change it. Judgment belongs to Allah, and the upright religion builds values. He explains Yusuf's interpretation, why he did not lecture the cupbearer on wine, the two views on who forgot to mention Yusuf, and how patience can turn into entitlement, as he sees in patients with terminal cancer, whereas Yusuf stayed content for years. He ends with the king's dream of fat and lean cows.

outline.heading: Yusuf credits his knowledge to his Lord
outline.gist: Righteous people attribute their knowledge to Allah, who arranged their teachers and circumstances, unlike the arrogant self that wants praise.

outline.heading: Leaving a creed by conviction, not inheritance
outline.gist: He examined his captors' beliefs before leaving them, and followed his fathers' religion because he found it better.

outline.heading: Tawhid as a favour to us and to all people
outline.gist: Its benefit reaches society as a whole, but most people do not give thanks for it.

outline.heading: The etiquette of answering: invite first
outline.gist: Yusuf promises to answer before their food arrives, but first explains where his knowledge comes from.

outline.heading: Scattered lords or Allah the One?
outline.gist: 'Companions of the prison' is gentle address; serving many quarrelling masters scatters a life, as in the parable of the man with partners.

outline.heading: Why humans keep falling into shirk
outline.gist: The difference between a monotheist and a polytheist society is behavioural, economic and social, and many nominally monotheist societies are not truly so.

outline.heading: Tawhid gives fixed morals
outline.gist: Morals from one source do not change; the Prophet, the Quran walking on earth, is the model.

outline.heading: Bribes, connections and favours
outline.gist: A system of many gatekeepers lets you bend the law through wasta; we dislike the upright official who will not bend.

outline.heading: Shirk in ethics: the shahadah as prestige
outline.gist: Saying la ilaha illa Allah while ethics follow self-interest makes the creed mere prestige.

outline.heading: Divine versus human sources of morality
outline.gist: Monotheist ethics stay the same across centuries; human-sourced ethics can be good but do not hold without tawhid.

outline.heading: A radical change: from bribable idols to clear law
outline.gist: Pre-Islamic Arabs chose gods and judges who could be bought; tawhid replaces this with a clear law.

outline.heading: Al-Qahhar: the true Subduer
outline.gist: All three were oppressed in prison; the jailer is himself subdued, and only Allah subdues all.

outline.heading: Lords are whatever you submit to blindly
outline.gist: In the Quran a lord or god is anything one obeys blindly, including one's own desire.

outline.heading: Islam: surrendering only to Allah
outline.gist: Submitting yourself to a cleric, a tree and its keeper, or your desire is shirk.

outline.heading: What a 'name' is
outline.gist: A word that carries a meaning between minds; Adam was taught names and humans were taught expression.

outline.heading: Worshipping an aura: the ribboned tree
outline.gist: No one worships a tree itself but the name and halo built around it, like a tree in Syria hung with ribbons for fertility.

outline.heading: Pharaoh and rulers as inflated names
outline.gist: Pharaoh was an ordinary man given a name and an aura; rulers too are ordinary people behind their titles.

outline.heading: No authority sent down: fear none but Allah
outline.gist: Everything Allah revealed says there is no god but Him, so do not humiliate yourself to anyone else.

outline.heading: Why tyrants prefer submissive religion
outline.gist: A person who fears only Allah is dangerous to tyrants, who fund passive religiosity and silence those who tell people to use their minds.

outline.heading: Tawhid demands caring about wrong
outline.gist: Accepting corruption and saying 'stay by the wall' shows a deficiency in tawhid; at least reject wrong in the heart.

outline.heading: Unable to speak versus not caring
outline.gist: Someone silenced who still seeks change differs from one indifferent or complicit; he lived there and saw both.

outline.heading: Judgment belongs to Allah alone
outline.gist: Allah, not people, decides what is permitted, forbidden and moral.

outline.heading: The upright religion that builds values
outline.gist: Al-din al-qayyim comes from the roots of setting straight and of values: religion rests on morals.

outline.heading: 'Most people do not know': no contempt
outline.gist: Yusuf shows no hatred; people fail to thank or know, so we try to bring the knowledge to them.

outline.heading: Recitation of the passage
outline.gist: He recites the interpretation, Yusuf's request and the king's dream.

outline.heading: Dawah came before the answer
outline.gist: Wronged and suffering in prison, Yusuf used his moment to call the two youths to Allah.

outline.heading: 'He will serve his lord wine'
outline.gist: Rabb here means the king, the master of the house; the word has many uses in Arabic.

outline.heading: Why Yusuf did not lecture him on wine
outline.gist: He prioritised tawhid over secondary rulings, linked to the debate on whether disbelievers are addressed by the branches of law; no revealed law ever permitted wine.

outline.heading: The other will be crucified
outline.gist: Crucifixion was an ancient deterrent; he skips reports on why the two were imprisoned as distractions.

outline.heading: The matter is decreed
outline.gist: The word for seeking a fatwa appears here; reports say the one executed had accepted Yusuf's call.

outline.heading: 'Remember me to your lord'
outline.gist: Yusuf 'thought' the man would be saved, since only Allah knows the unseen, and asked him to mention his wrongful imprisonment.

outline.heading: First view: the freed man forgot
outline.gist: The stronger view is that Shaytan made the freed man forget to mention Yusuf to the king.

outline.heading: Several years in prison
outline.gist: Bid' means three to nine; seven or nine years is close to a decade of a young man's life.

outline.heading: Second view: Yusuf relied on a man
outline.gist: He rejects the view that Yusuf was disciplined for relying on the freed man, but values the exegetes' flexibility about human nature.

outline.heading: When patience turns into entitlement
outline.gist: Those tested often expect relief as payment for their patience.

outline.heading: Patients facing terminal illness
outline.gist: Patients who accept their diagnosis still expect to be spared; true reliance means preparing wills and mending ties.

outline.heading: Yusuf: nine years of contentment
outline.gist: No lawyer or appeal, yet he stayed patient and content: that is sabr, rida and tawakkul.

outline.heading: Do not burden us beyond our strength
outline.gist: Why we pray the closing dua of Al-Baqarah: we may not bear what Yusuf bore.

outline.heading: The Hyksos king
outline.gist: The king was one of the shepherd kings, closer to the Arabs and to tawhid than the Copts, and a just man like the Negus.

outline.heading: The king's dream of cows and ears of grain
outline.gist: A recurring dream; dreams may reflect what the king sensed of the economy without connecting it.

outline.heading: Outro

yIKVbO8HD-4.title: English Tafseer: Surat Al-Infitar 1-19
yIKVbO8HD-4.one_line: Al-Infitar as the second step in the free-will cluster: our choices are not only sacred but recorded, so we must own them.
yIKVbO8HD-4.summary: He places Al-Infitar in the cluster of five surahs on freedom of choice: Al-Takwir taught that human will is a sacred gift, and this surah adds that every choice is recorded. Humans alone can think about their thinking, and no one can take away the inner choice to accept or reject. After the cosmic upheavals of the opening verses, every soul knows what it sent forward and held back, in all senses of those words. As a physician he stresses that what is not documented cannot be proven, and that most disputes come down to unrecorded claims. The wife of al-Aziz shows the minimum honesty of not betraying the truth inside oneself, whereas people who convince themselves of their own lies will even swear falsely to Allah. Verse 6 asks what deceived man about his generous Lord; the answer is not deception but denial of the Day of Reckoning, since no one who truly believed every choice would be questioned could live carelessly. Noble, trustworthy recorders write everything. The surah ends with the virtuous in bliss and the wicked in fire. He condemns today's culture of victimhood and of lying about intentions, and urges a generation that takes full responsibility for its choices.

outline.heading: The free-will cluster and human uniqueness
